core.text: Two tiny words never stand alone but are glued to the end of another word: **the tacked-on words -que ('and') and -ne (turns a sentence into a question)**, *encliticae -que, -ne*. *-que* joins the word it sits on to what came before: *puerī puellaeque* = boys and girls, with the 'and' hanging off *puellae*. *-ne* sits on the first word of a sentence and makes it a yes/no question: *Estne Gallia in Eurōpā?* = Is Gaul in Europe?
English asks a yes/no question by moving the verb to the front (*is* Gaul in Europe?). Latin keeps the order and adds *-ne* to the word it asks about.
-que = 'and', added to the second of the two things joined; -ne on the first word = a yes/no question. Read the word without its tail first.

invented.en: Julius and Aemilia live in the villa.

core.text: The tail *-ne* is not the word *nē* (so that … not; don't). *-ne* is short, glued on, and asks; *nē* stands on its own with a long vowel, opens a clause and forbids: *Venitne?* — is he coming? *Nē veniat!* — let him not come.

teach.title: A word glued to the end of another
teach.say: Latin has a few words too small to stand on their own, so they ride on the back of the word in front: the tacked-on words -que ('and') and -ne (turns a sentence into a question). In *Sicilia Sardiniaque īnsulae magnae sunt* the word is *Sardinia* with *-que* stuck on the end. Read the word without its tail first, then add what the tail means.

teach.title: -que means ‘and’
teach.say: *-que* ties its own word to what came before, so the ‘and’ hangs on the second of the two things joined: *Gallia Hispāniaque* is Gaul and Spain. English puts ‘and’ between them; Latin sticks it onto the end of the second.

teach.title: -ne asks a yes-or-no question
teach.say: *-ne* is glued to the word the question is really about, and that word moves to the front — most often the verb: *Nīlus fluvius magnus est* becomes *Estne Nīlus fluvius magnus…?* English asks in the same way, by putting the verb first; Latin puts it first and adds the tail. When the question is about something else, that word leads instead: *Aegyptusne prōvincia Rōmāna est?* asks whether it is Egypt that is a Roman province.

teach.title: Not every -que is ‘and’
teach.say: *Quoque* means ‘also’ and is one whole word, not *quo* plus *-que*. When a word ends in -que, ask whether what is left in front of it is a word you know: *Sardinia* is, *quo* is not.

teach.title: The word under the tail keeps its own job
teach.say: A tail adds a meaning and changes nothing else. In *Suntne Sicilia Sardiniaque īnsulae magnae?*, *Sardiniaque* is still plain *Sardinia*, still one of the things the sentence is about, and *Suntne* is still *sunt*, ‘are’. Strip the tail, read the word, then put the tail’s meaning back.

more.text: The learner's notes have only a heading for this topic (week 18), so the fuller picture comes from Ørberg and Allen & Greenough. A third enclitic, *-ve*, means 'or'. All three throw the word's stress onto the syllable just before them (*puellae-QUE*).

Not every word ending in -que is 'and' plus a word: *quoque* (also), *neque* (and not), *itaque* (therefore), *ubīque* (everywhere) and *-cumque* words are whole words. *-que* can join two sentences as well as two words, sitting on the first word of the second: Julius sees Quintus *eumque interrogat* — and asks him (r03:53.1). *-ne* attaches to *nōn* to make *nōnne*, which expects the answer yes; *num* (Num Crēta oppidum est?) expects no. Ørberg cap. I (-ne, -que), cap. III (-que on a pronoun); A&G §121, §332.

sources: Ørberg cap. I & III Grammatica Latina
